Spot Markets for AI Inference
Dynamic Capacity Allocation and Pricing on a Shared Accelerator Fleet
Quanyan Zhu
Tandon School of Engineering, New York University, Brooklyn, NY, USA
qz494@nyu.edu
abstract
Inference providers size their accelerator fleets for the interactive peak and sell spare capacity through fixed
discounts, such as batch tiers at half price. However, inference differs from conventional cloud capacity in four
respects: capacity depends on the latency tier through batching, moving weights between models is slow and
costly, spot demand can wait until its deadline, and power can bind. In this paper, we develop a framework for
dynamic capacity allocation and pricing of AI inference on a shared accelerator fleet. We consider a provider
that serves several models under a power cap and sells each model in an interactive tier with a speed promise
and in a spot tier for preemptible work with a deadline. In each period, the provider chooses how many replicas
of each model to keep loaded and what spot price to quote. We show that one interactive token displaces
a fixed number 𝜌𝑚> 1 of spot tokens, and that the optimal spot price lies midway between the interactive
price and the effective cost of capacity in the deadline window, which is close to the prevailing half price only
when the fleet is slack. We further show that a spot tier raises the optimal reliability of the interactive tier,
and that placement should follow persistent demand shifts while prices absorb transients. Building on these
results, we design a model predictive controller based on a linear program with explicit approximation bounds,
which solves each period in milliseconds. Numerical experiments on a simulated week with a measured daily
demand profile, a flash crowd, and a grid curtailment show that the controller raises profit by 7.4% over fixed
half-price practice, captures 93% of the gain available with perfect forecasts, keeps the interactive promise
through both events, and leaves spot buyers better off.
Keywords: AI inference; spot pricing; capacity allocation; accelerator fleets; batching; model predictive
control; power caps
1 Introduction
Generative AI is increasingly delivered as a metered service. When a person, an application, or
an autonomous agent submits a request to a foundation model, the model produces its response
one token at a time on a fleet of specialized accelerators, and the provider charges for the tokens
consumed [10, 49]. As foundation models become embedded in search, software development,
customer service, and multi-step agentic workflows, the production of tokens, known as inference,
has emerged as a central economic activity of the AI industry. Inference is also intensive in both
1
arXiv:2611.11215v1  [eess.SY]  8 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
capital and energy. The accelerators that perform inference are among the most expensive assets
in computing, and the data centers that house them have become a rapidly growing source of
electricity demand [17, 37]. Therefore, the allocation and pricing of inference capacity is not only
an engineering question of throughput and latency but also an economic question about the use of a
scarce, costly, and perishable resource.
Inference capacity differs from a conventional commodity in three respects. First, it is perishable.
An accelerator-hour that is not used to generate tokens cannot be stored and sold later, and hence
idle capacity is a cost that is never recovered. Second, it is slow to reconfigure. To serve a model,
a provider must load the model’s weights, often tens to hundreds of gigabytes, onto one or more
accelerators, which takes from seconds to minutes and interrupts production on those accelerators
[13]. Third, the quantity of capacity depends on the quality of service that it delivers. Serving
systems process many requests together in a batch [19, 45], and a larger batch produces more tokens
per second in total but fewer for each request [30]. As a result, a provider that promises interactive
users a fast stream of tokens must keep its batches small and accept a lower throughput than the
same hardware could deliver for work that can tolerate delay.
These properties shape how inference is provisioned and sold today. Interactive demand follows
the working day of its users. Since weights cannot be loaded quickly enough to meet a sudden
surge, providers size their fleets for the busiest hour with a margin for forecast error. Consequently, a
substantial part of the fleet idles for much of the day. The major providers have responded by selling
deferrable work at a discount. Batch interfaces complete requests within a day at half the standard
price, flex tiers offer lower prices in exchange for slower or less reliable service, and some providers
have charged less in off-peak hours [4, 9, 15, 26, 27]. One important feature shared by these offers
is that their prices are fixed. In other words, the prices do not respond to whether the fleet is busy or
idle, and access is rationed through rate limits and queues rather than through prices.
At the same time, the conditions under which inference capacity is supplied are becoming more
variable. The release of a new model can raise demand for it sharply within hours. Agents, evaluation
suites, and data pipelines generate large volumes of work that can wait minutes or hours for an
answer. Moreover, data centers are increasingly constrained by their connections to the power grid,
and grid operators are asking large loads to reduce consumption at short notice [17, 25]. A fixed
discount cannot respond to any of these conditions. When the fleet is slack, a fixed discount may
be close to the right price. When the fleet is tight, however, it leaves the scarcity value of capacity
unpriced, and when the grid is stressed, it provides no signal that would move flexible work to other
hours. Nevertheless, a dynamic alternative is not straightforward to design. The provider must decide
which models to keep loaded and at what price to sell spare capacity before it observes the next
period’s interactive load, and it must honor the deadlines of the work that it has already accepted.
Infrastructure clouds faced a related problem when they began to sell idle virtual machines. Spot
instances, introduced in 2009, offered spare capacity at a price that varied with its availability [1, 3],
and a body of work has studied how a data-center operator can adapt its capacity, and in spot markets
also its prices, to changing demand [18, 21, 46]. However, inference differs from virtual machines in
ways that change the structure of the control problem. Two of these differences have been noted
above. The capacity of a replica depends on the latency tier that it serves, and moving accelerators
between models is slow and costly, even though dividing a model’s replicas between tiers is a free
setting of the batch scheduler. Two further differences arise from the nature of demand and supply.
Spot work has a deadline rather than a start time, so demand can wait while capacity cannot. In
addition, power, not only the number of accelerators, can limit production. Section 2 explains each
of these features in more detail.
2


--- Page 3 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
In this paper, we develop a framework for dynamic capacity allocation and pricing of AI inference
on a shared accelerator fleet. We consider a provider that serves several models under a power cap
and sells each model in two tiers: an interactive tier, at a posted price with a guaranteed decode
speed, and a spot tier, for preemptible work that must be completed within a deadline, at a price
that the provider may revise every period. In each period, the provider decides how many replicas
of each model to keep loaded and what spot price to quote before the period’s interactive load is
realized. The resulting problem is a constrained stochastic control problem with two time scales, a
queue with deadlines, and coupling across models through the shared fleet and the power cap. We
first study simplified versions of the problem that admit closed-form characterizations, and we then
solve the full problem by model predictive control. Figure 1 illustrates the setting and its translation
into control-theoretic terms.
The contributions of this paper are fourfold. First, we show that continuous batching induces a
latency exchange rate between the two tiers. At the margin, one interactive token per second displaces
𝜌𝑚> 1 spot tokens per second, where 𝜌𝑚is the ratio of a replica’s full-load throughputs at the two
tiers’ batch caps (Lemma 1). This result converts the latency premium of interactive service into a
linear capacity constraint that can be priced.
Second, we characterize optimal spot prices. On a shared fleet, the optimal spot price lies midway
between the interactive price and the full marginal cost of a spot token, which includes the shadow
rents of the fleet and of power. These rents are determined by water-filling across models, and hence
a demand surge on one model raises the spot prices of all models (Proposition 1). When the fleet is
slack, the rule reproduces the half-price discount observed in practice, and a fixed discount loses
little. When the fleet is tight, however, a fixed discount forgoes the scarcity rent (Proposition 2).
When work can be deferred, the relevant cost is that of the cheapest capacity within the deadline
window (Theorem 1).
Third, we establish two structural results on reliability and placement. A spot tier acts as a salvage
market for the safety capacity of the interactive tier and therefore raises the optimal reliability of
interactive service (Theorem 2). Moreover, placement exhibits an inaction band determined by the
round-trip cost of loading and unloading a model. In other words, transient shocks are absorbed by
prices, and only persistent shifts justify moving weights (Theorem 3).
Fourth, we design a model predictive controller that embeds these results. A piecewise-linear
approximation of revenue, tangent cuts on the expected interactive overflow, and a cumulative
representation of deadlines reduce each period’s planning problem to a linear program with explicit
approximation bounds (Lemmas 2 and 3). The program solves in about 7 milliseconds (Section 6).
We evaluate the controller on a simulated week of a 512-accelerator fleet serving three models,
with a daily demand profile measured on a public inference marketplace, a flash crowd triggered by
a model launch, and a curtailment requested by the grid operator (Section 7). Relative to a strong
version of current practice, the controller raises profit by 7.4% and captures 93% of the gain available
to a controller with perfect forecasts. It keeps the interactive speed promise through both events,
serves more spot work, and increases the surplus of spot buyers. Note that the sources of the gain
differ across regimes. On ordinary days, the gain comes mainly from prices, whereas during the two
events it comes from reallocating accelerators and power across models. Collectively, these results
suggest that a spot tier with dynamic prices is more than a channel for selling idle capacity. It also
serves as an instrument for managing the reliability of interactive service, absorbing demand shocks,
and offering flexibility to the power grid.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes how inference capacity is
produced and sold and states the problem. Section 3 reviews related work. Section 4 presents
3

the model, and Section 5 characterizes optimal policies in simplified settings. Section 6 develops
the model predictive controller, and Section 7 reports the numerical study. Section 8 discusses
implications and limitations, and Section 9 concludes the paper. Proofs are collected in Appendix A.
2 Background and problem statement
In this section, we describe how inference capacity is produced and sold, explain why a substantial
part of it idles, and identify the features that distinguish its allocation from that of conventional cloud
capacity. We conclude the section with a statement of the problem studied in the rest of the paper.
Figure 1 summarizes the setting pictorially and restates the problem in the vocabulary of stochastic
control for readers who are familiar with the methods but new to AI inference.
Production of inference. A provider serves a model by loading a copy of its weights, called a replica,
onto one or more accelerators. A small dense model may fit on a single accelerator, whereas a large
mixture-of-experts model may span eight or more. A request is processed in two phases. In the
prefill phase, the replica reads the prompt and builds a key–value cache that summarizes it. In the
decode phase, it generates the response one token at a time, and each token requires a pass through
the whole model. Note that, for the batch sizes used in interactive service, a decode step is limited
by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic, since it must read the weights and the caches of all
sequences in progress [30]. Therefore, serving systems process many sequences together so that one
pass over the weights advances every sequence in the batch by one token. With continuous batching,
sequences join and leave the batch at every step [45], and paged memory management allows the
caches of many sequences to share the accelerator’s memory [19]. A larger batch raises the total
throughput of a replica but slows every sequence in it, since each step takes longer. In other words,
the batch size is an operating point on a trade-off between throughput and latency, and it is bounded
above by the memory available for caches. Section 4.1 formalizes this trade-off.
Fleet sizing for the peak. Interactive demand follows the working day of its users. On one public
inference marketplace, the hourly token volume over 30 days has a peak-to-trough ratio of 2.6 across
the hours of the day [32]. Since weights cannot be loaded quickly enough to meet a surge, a provider
must keep enough replicas loaded to serve interactive traffic at its busiest hour with a margin for
forecast error. A fleet sized for the peak of this profile runs at 69% utilization on average, and at
63% with a 10% safety margin. In the fleet simulated in Section 7, mean interactive load occupies
49% of the accelerators on average, ranging between 33% and 68% over the day. The remaining
accelerators represent capacity that the provider has already paid for. Note that accelerators are
expensive to own or lease, and an accelerator-hour that is not used cannot be recovered later.
Fixed discounts for spare capacity. The major providers sell deferral through batch interfaces that
complete work within a day at half the standard price [4, 15, 26]. Some providers also sell flex tiers,
which may be slower or unavailable at busy times, and priority tiers, which cost more [5, 27]. One
provider has charged lower prices in off-peak hours [9]. Across the tiered endpoints listed on one
large model router on 31 October 2026, the median flex price is 0.50 of the standard price of the
same model and provider, the median priority price is 2.00, and the median batch price is 0.50 [28].
These ratios are round numbers set by policy. They do not change when the fleet is busy or idle, and
batch tiers ration access with rate limits and queues rather than with prices. Moreover, secondary
venues on which inference capacity is resold quote prices well below list [31, 41]. This situation
resembles the early market for cloud capacity before spot instances priced spare virtual machines
according to their availability [1, 3].

Spot Markets for AI Inference
Distinctive features of inference capacity. Dynamic pricing of spare capacity is well established for
virtual machines. However, four features of inference change the control problem.
1. Capacity depends on the service tier. A replica’s throughput rises with its batch size, and the latency
promise of the interactive tier caps the batch. Hence, the same replica produces more spot tokens
than interactive tokens, and one interactive token displaces 𝜌𝑚> 1 spot tokens (Lemma 1). In
contrast, a virtual machine is a fixed unit of capacity regardless of what it is sold as.
2. Placement is slow and costly, while splitting between tiers is free. Moving an accelerator from one
model to another requires loading tens to hundreds of gigabytes of weights, which takes seconds
for a small model and minutes for a large one [13]. In contrast, dividing a model’s replicas
between interactive and spot work is a setting of the batch scheduler [19, 45]. As a result, the
control problem has two time scales.
3. Demand can be stored, but capacity cannot. Spot work has a deadline rather than a start time, and
hence admitted work waits in a backlog. The backlog is a state variable, and the right price for
spot work in the current period depends on the capacity that will be free before its deadline.
4. Power, not only accelerators, can bind. Inference facilities are increasingly limited by their grid
connections, and grid operators are asking large loads to curtail at short notice [17, 25, 37].
Spot work is the part of the load that can be curtailed without breaking a promise, as long as its
deadlines can still be met.
The problem
Consider a provider that serves several models on one fleet of accelerators under a power cap. The
provider sells each model in an interactive tier, at a posted price with a speed promise, and in a spot
tier, for preemptible work with a deadline, at a price that it may change every period. In every period, it
chooses how many replicas of each model to keep loaded and what spot price to quote before it knows the
period’s interactive load. The problem is to determine how the provider should set placement and prices
to maximize profit, keep the interactive promise, and meet spot deadlines, when loading a model takes
time and money, spot work can wait, and power may be curtailed.
Significance of the problem. The problem is important for three reasons. First, the stakes are large.
Accelerator fleets are among the most expensive assets in computing, and hence a few percentage
points of their utilization represent substantial value. Second, the problem is becoming more
pressing. Much of the work that agents and data pipelines generate, such as evaluations, synthetic
data, document processing, and overnight agent runs, does not need an answer within seconds. In
addition, data centers are becoming the loads that grid operators ask to flex [17, 25]. Third, a spot
price that reflects the scarcity of capacity carries information beyond a single transaction. It tells
buyers when flexible work is cheap to run, informs the facility of how much load it can shed when
the grid is stressed, and provides a reference price on which forward contracts, capacity reservations,
and other instruments for inference capacity can be written. In contrast, a fixed discount conveys
none of this information.
3 Related work
In this section, we review related work on cloud spot markets, language-model serving, revenue
management, electricity markets, model predictive control, and AI economics.
6


--- Page 7 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
Spot markets for cloud capacity. Spot instances sell the idle capacity of an infrastructure cloud
at a price that varies with its availability. Agmon Ben-Yehuda et al. [1] have found that early spot
prices were not always set by an open market, and Amazon Web Services later replaced bidding
with smoothed prices [3]. On the provider’s side, our previous work [46] has formulated capacity
allocation and pricing for the spot markets of an infrastructure cloud as a constrained optimal control
problem solved by model predictive control, and Zhang et al. [47] have studied dynamic service
placement across data centers with reconfiguration costs. We adopt the receding-horizon architecture
of this line of work but change the plant: capacity depends on the service tier through batching,
demand can wait in a backlog with deadlines, capacity changes have explicit costs, and power is a
constraint. Our provider sets prices openly as a monopolist of its own spare capacity, and Remark 1
gives its competitive ask. On the buyer’s side of a spot market, Miao et al. [24] serve language models
on preemptible instances.
Serving language models. Continuous batching [45], paged key–value caches [19], chunked prefill
[2], and disaggregated prefill and decode [29, 48] raise the throughput of a replica and make the
throughput–latency trade-off explicit, as analyzed by Pope et al. [30]. Our batching law and the
exchange rate 𝜌𝑚summarize this trade-off for the controller. AlpaServe [20] places models on a
shared cluster to exploit statistical multiplexing, and ServerlessLLM [13] reduces the cost of loading
a model. These systems decide placement for a given demand. In contrast, we add prices and a
deferrable tier, and we treat loading time and cost as frictions whose economic effect is characterized
by Theorem 3.
Revenue management and peak-load pricing. Selling a perishable capacity to price-sensitive
demand is the problem of revenue management [14, 40]. One key difference in our setting is that
the capacity regenerates every period, its size is a decision, and it is shared across products at a rate
that depends on the product. Peak-load pricing [8, 38] explains why the price of capacity should rise
when it is scarce. Proposition 1 is a monopoly version with several products sharing one plant, and
Theorem 1 adds storable demand. The backfill theorem is a newsvendor result [6] in which the spot
tier serves as the salvage market for safety capacity.
Electricity markets and data-center flexibility. Spot pricing of electricity over space and time
[7, 39, 44] provides the model for pricing a non-storable good from a constrained network. Data
centers can shift workload in time to follow electricity prices or carbon intensity [33, 34, 43] and
reduce their demand during grid peaks [22]. Dynamic right-sizing turns servers off when load is
low and faces the same switching costs as our placement problem [21]. Lookahead control of data
centers goes back at least to Kusic et al. [18]. Our contribution to this line of work is to price the
flexibility. The spot tier is the curtailable part of the load, and its price tells buyers when curtailment
is likely.
Model predictive control. Receding-horizon control of constrained systems has a mature theory
[23, 35]. We use it as a practical method and do not claim stability or optimality guarantees for
the closed loop. Instead, the numerical study measures how close it comes to a controller with
perfect forecasts. Note that the inaction bands of Theorem 3 are the discrete-time analog of those in
investment under adjustment costs [11, 12].
The economics of AI inference. Demirer et al. [10] document the pricing, supply, and demand of
language-model inference, and in Zhu [49], we have studied the economics of tokens, computation,
and pricing in foundation models. These studies take the provider’s capacity and costs as given or
focus on posted prices. In contrast, this paper takes the provider’s side. We derive the cost of capacity
7


--- Page 8 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
from the fleet, its batching, and its power supply, and we show what spot price a provider should
quote as a result.
4 The model
In this section, we present the model of the fleet, the demand, and the dynamics, and we formulate
the provider’s control problem. We divide time into control periods 𝑡= 0, 1, . . . of length Δ seconds,
and we set Δ = 15 minutes in the numerical study. Within a period, the set of loaded replicas is fixed,
but the scheduler can change, at every decode step, which sequences share a batch. Therefore, the
model has two layers: a slow layer of placement, decided at the start of each period, and a fast layer
of batching inside the period, which we summarize by its throughput.
Placement and batching correspond to layers 2 and 3 of Fig. 2, which places them within a
broader view of the provider’s operations, from the hardware at the bottom to the buyers at the top.
Capacity is built up from the accelerators through the deployments, the serving engine, and the
queues, and it is sold as products and tiers to buyers whose demand responds to price and latency.
For each layer, the figure indicates its time scale and the elements of the model that represent it.
Two features of the figure deserve emphasis. First, changing a deployment, which requires loading
weights and warming caches, is a transition within layer 2 rather than a layer of its own; the model
captures it through the loading time 𝐿𝑚and the costs 𝜅±
𝑚. Second, the controller acts on only two
layers, the placement and the spot price, and it observes the others.
4.1 Fleet, models, and batching
Consider a provider that operates a fleet of 𝐺identical accelerators in one facility with a power cap of
𝑊𝑡kilowatts. The provider serves a set M = {1, . . . , 𝑀} of models. A replica of model 𝑚refers to one
loaded copy of its weights, and it occupies 𝑔𝑚accelerators (e.g., one accelerator for a small dense
model and eight for a large mixture-of-experts model).
Decode. We adopt a first-order model of memory-bound decode [30]. In each step, a replica reads
its weights once and the key–value cache of every sequence in its batch. Hence, a decode step of a
replica that holds a batch of 𝑏sequences takes

Figure 2. A layered view of inference supply and demand, from the hardware at the bottom to the buyers
at the top. Capacity is built up through the four supply layers (gray), and demand reaches down from the
two market layers (orange). Each layer is labeled with its time scale and with the elements of the model that
represent it. The controller of Section 6 acts on two layers, through the placement (the slow lever) and the
spot price (the fast lever), and it observes the others. Changing a deployment is a transition within layer 2
rather than a layer of its own, and switching between models in layer 6 lies outside the scope of the model.

4.2 Demand
Interactive load. Let 𝑅𝑚,𝑡denote the average rate, in tokens per second, at which interactive traffic
for model 𝑚arrives during period 𝑡. This rate is random, and the provider forecasts it with mean ˆ𝑟𝑚,𝑡
and standard deviation 𝜎𝑚,𝑡(Section 6.1). Each interactive token that is served earns 𝜋𝑚. A token
that cannot be served at the promised speed is lost and incurs a penalty 𝛽𝑚in service credits and
goodwill.
Spot demand. In period 𝑡, a population of spot buyers for model 𝑚would buy Λ𝑚,𝑡tokens of work
at a price of zero. Their valuations per token are uniform on [0, 𝜋𝑚], so that no buyer pays more for
deferrable service than the interactive price at which it could buy immediate service. At spot price 𝑝,
the work admitted is
𝑎𝑚,𝑡= Λ𝑚,𝑡(1 −𝑝/𝜋𝑚)+,
equivalently
𝑝= 𝜋𝑚(1 −𝑎𝑚,𝑡/Λ𝑚,𝑡).
(3)
Linear demand is a common choice in the pricing of cloud capacity [46]. It keeps the pricing rules
in closed form, and its slope 𝛼𝑚,𝑡= Λ𝑚,𝑡/𝜋𝑚scales with the size of the buyer population. Note that
spot revenue 𝑎𝜋𝑚(1 −𝑎/Λ𝑚,𝑡) is a concave quadratic in the admitted volume, while every constraint
of the model is linear in it. Therefore, we optimize over admissions and recover the price from the
demand curve.
10


--- Page 11 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
Deadlines. Work admitted in period 𝑡must be completed by the end of period 𝑡+ 𝐷−1. Work
that misses its deadline expires, its price is refunded, and the provider pays a penalty 𝛾𝑚per token.
This convention matches current batch interfaces, which do not charge for requests that expire [26].
While admitted work waits, the provider incurs a small holding cost ℎ𝑚per token per period, which
captures the buyers’ preference for earlier completion and breaks ties in favor of serving early. The
deadline 𝐷is a contract term. For example, 𝐷= 1 corresponds to a spot tier with no deferral, 𝐷= 8
(two hours) is in the range of current flex tiers, and 𝐷= 96 (a day) corresponds to a batch tier.

4.4 The control problem
At the start of period 𝑡, the provider knows the history up to 𝑡−1, namely, past loads, the backlog with
its deadlines, and the replicas in place. It also knows the announced electricity prices and power caps.
The provider then chooses the placement 𝑛𝑡= (𝑛𝑚,𝑡)𝑚and the spot prices 𝑝𝑡= (𝑝𝑚,𝑡)𝑚. Afterwards,
interactive load 𝑅𝑡and the spot intercepts Λ𝑡are realized, interactive traffic is served, and the spot
backlog is served within the remaining capacity and power. The provider’s problem is formulated as
max
non-anticipative (𝑛𝑡,𝑝𝑡) 𝔼

𝑡=0
𝐽𝑡
i
subject to (3)–(8).
(P)
Figure 4 illustrates the feedback loop. Problem (P) is a constrained stochastic control problem. Its
state, which includes the replicas, the backlog by deadline, and the forecast state, is too large for
exact dynamic programming. Moreover, its controls interact through the shared fleet and power cap,
and its dynamics have two time scales. Therefore, Section 5 first studies deterministic and one-period
versions of the problem to learn what optimal policies look like, and Section 6 then solves (P) by
model predictive control.
5 Structure of optimal policies
In this section, we study four simplified versions of (P). Each version isolates one feature of the
inference setting, namely, a shared fleet whose capacity depends on the tier, storable demand, random

interactive load, and costly placement. The results explain the behavior of the controller of Section 6,
and they provide the provider with pricing rules that can be published.

Proof. See Appendix A.3.
Part (v) offers an interpretation of current practice. When the fleet is slack, the monopoly price
for spare capacity is half the interactive price, up to a negligible energy term (Table 1). This is
exactly the 50% discount that current batch tiers charge [4, 15, 26]. Note that the result depends
on the assumption that valuations are uniform up to the interactive price, and hence it should not
be interpreted as a structural law. Nevertheless, it does indicate where a fixed half-price rule goes
wrong, namely, when the fleet is tight. In this case, 𝜈> 0, and the optimal spot price rises above
half the interactive price by 1
2𝑔𝑚𝜈/(Δ𝜃S
𝑚). Part (iv) shows that this happens for every model at once
since the models share the fleet. For example, a launch-day surge on the large model raises the spot
price of the small one, even though no small-model buyer has changed its behavior. Virtual machine
types in a cloud spot market share a data center in the same way. One key difference is that the rate
at which one virtual machine type displaces another is fixed by the machine size, whereas here it
depends on the latency tier through 𝜌𝑚. Therefore, part (ii) also gives the provider a pricing floor for
its interactive tier, i.e., 𝜋𝑚≥𝜌𝑚MC𝑚.
Proposition 2 (What a fixed discount loses). Fix one model and one period, and let 𝑐denote the
marginal cost of a spot token, including any shadow price of capacity at the optimum. Let 𝑝∗denote the
optimal spot price and ¯𝑝any other price.
(i) If capacity binds at neither price, the loss from charging ¯𝑝is Λ
𝜋(¯𝑝−𝑝∗)2. Over periods 𝑡= 1, . . . , 𝑇
in which this holds, a fixed price ¯𝑝loses Í
𝑡𝛼𝑡(¯𝑝−𝑝∗
𝑡)2 ≥␀Í
𝑡𝛼𝑡
 Var𝛼(𝑝∗), where 𝛼𝑡= Λ𝑡/𝜋and
Var𝛼is the 𝛼-weighted variance of the optimal price path.
(ii) If capacity 𝐾binds at the optimum, so that 𝑝∗is the market-clearing price, a lower price ¯𝑝< 𝑝∗
with admissions rationed to 𝐾loses (𝑝∗−¯𝑝) 𝐾, i.e., the whole scarcity rent on the gap.
Proof. See Appendix A.4.
Therefore, the loss from a fixed discount is second order in slack periods and first order in tight
periods. In other words, a half-price rule is close to optimal when there is spare capacity, whereas
in tight periods it gives up the full scarcity rent while rate limits ration access. Figure 5 illustrates
both regimes on the calibrated fleet. The same asymmetry underlies the classical case for peak-load
pricing [8, 38], and it has been noted for flat-rate charging of cloud capacity, which is inefficient
both when demand is far below capacity and when it exceeds capacity [46].

Figure 5. One-period spot prices on a shared fleet (Proposition 1), computed for each hour of a Monday at
mean demand, with 𝐷= 1 and no switching costs. (a) The shadow rent 𝜈of the fleet is zero except in the 4
evening hours in which the fleet binds, and it peaks at $1.51 per accelerator-hour at 22 : 00 UTC. (b) Optimal

hours. (c) Spillover. At the peak hour, scaling the interactive load of the large model alone raises the spot price
of every model. At 1.5 times its load, the spot prices of the small and medium models rise by 31% and 31%.

2 (𝜋+ 𝐶𝑡), and every period with 𝑎𝑡= 0 has 𝐶𝑡≥𝜋;
(ii) work admitted in period 𝑡can be scheduled so that it is served only in periods that attain the
minimum in (14);
(iii) if capacity is slack in some period 𝜏∈W𝑡(𝜇𝜏= 0), then 𝑝𝑡≤1
2
␀𝜋+ 𝑐𝜏+ ℎ(𝜏−𝑡);
(iv) optimal profit is nondecreasing in 𝐷.
Proof. See Appendix A.6.
Theorem 1 shows that a buyer who accepts a 𝐷-period deadline buys the cheapest capacity in its
window, valued at the shadow price of that later period plus the cost of waiting for it, and that the
provider passes half of the saving on in the price. With 𝐷= 1, 𝐶𝑡= 𝑐𝑡+ 𝜇𝑡, and the spot price follows
the current scarcity, as in Proposition 1. With a longer deadline, a peak-hour price is capped by an
off-peak cost (part iii, Fig. 6). In other words, deferral flattens spot prices and moves the scarcity
rent from peak periods to the slack periods that absorb the deferred work. Hence, a deadline is a
product attribute with a price. A buyer who is willing to wait buys capacity that would otherwise
idle, and the provider shares the saving through a lower price for longer deadlines.

The economics are those of the classic newsvendor [6], but the salvage value of unused capacity
is now provided by the spot market. When the spot market is liquid (𝑣high), safety capacity is cheap
to hold since whatever the interactive tier does not use is sold. Therefore, a provider with a spot tier
should promise, and deliver, better interactive service than one without (Fig. 7a). Amazon’s spot
instances sell the unused part of a fleet sized for on-demand and reserved customers in the same
way [1]. One key difference for inference is that the unused capacity is mostly the safety margin
of the interactive tier, and its size grows with the volatility of interactive demand (part iv). This is
the mechanism by which the controller of Section 6 sizes placements, since its expected-overflow
constraints embed (16).
5.4 Placement: pricing transients and placing trends

defined as the optimal value of that period’s pricing and service problem net of the rents. This function
is concave in 𝑛since that problem is a concave program in which 𝑛enters only through linear terms
(Lemma A.1 in Appendix A.1). The placement problem of one model is then given by

Part (iii) provides the operational rule, and Fig. 8 illustrates it. A transient that raises the marginal
value of an extra replica by 𝛿per period for 𝑑periods is not worth a reload when 𝑑𝛿is below the
round-trip cost. In this case, the provider absorbs the transient with the fast lever. The spot price
rises (Proposition 1(iv)), spot work is preempted and deferred within its deadline (Theorem 1), and
interactive traffic keeps its speed. Only persistent shifts, such as a regional daily cycle or a launch
that lasts for hours, justify moving weights. For large models, whose weights take minutes to load
and whose replicas span many accelerators, 𝜅± is large, and the band of inaction is wide. Note
that modeling switching through explicit load and unload costs, rather than a quadratic penalty
on capacity changes, yields the inaction bands familiar from investment under adjustment costs
[11, 12].

6 Model predictive control
In this section, we develop the model predictive controller. The controller applies the receding-horizon
principle of model predictive control [23, 35], which has been used to manage data centers and
cloud capacity [18, 46]. At the start of every period, the controller forecasts demand over the next 𝐻
periods, solves a deterministic program over that horizon, applies the first period’s placement and
prices, and repeats the procedure one period later with new information. Three features distinguish
the program from those used for virtual machine capacity. First, the program has to handle a queue
with deadlines. Second, the random interactive load enters through its expected overflow rather
than its mean. Third, capacity changes carry explicit costs rather than a quadratic penalty. All
three features can be expressed with linear constraints, and hence each period’s problem is a linear
program that solves in milliseconds.
6.1 Forecasts
For 𝑘= 0, . . . , 𝐻−1 steps ahead, the controller requires forecasts ˆ𝑟𝑚,𝑡+𝑘and 𝜎𝑚,𝑡+𝑘of the mean and
standard deviation of interactive load, a forecast ˆΛ𝑚,𝑡+𝑘of the spot intercept, and the electricity prices
and power caps that the grid operator has announced. In the numerical study, interactive load is a
seasonal profile ¯𝑅𝑚,𝑡times a multiplicative deviation, i.e., 𝑅𝑚,𝑡= ¯𝑅𝑚,𝑡(1 + 𝜖𝑚,𝑡), where 𝜖is a first-order
autoregression with coefficient 𝜙and stationary standard deviation 𝜍. The controller estimates the
current deviation from the last observed load and forecasts

The objective is the expected profit (9) with the exogenous interactive revenue Δ𝜋𝑚ˆ𝑟𝑚,𝑘dropped. In
this objective, each token of overflow loses its price and incurs its penalty. Similarly, expired work
loses its price, which is refunded, and incurs its penalty. The last three lines of constraints represent
the deadlines, the availability of work, and a terminal condition that the horizon end with an empty
backlog, which prevents the controller from pushing work beyond the horizon.
Lemma 2 (Deadlines as cumulative constraints). Fix one model, admissions 𝑎0, . . . , 𝑎𝐻−1, and an
initial backlog in which 𝑑𝑘units fall due by step 𝑘. Serve the backlog in first-in-first-out order. A sequence
of service and expiry (𝑥𝑘+ 𝑧𝑘)𝑘is feasible and completes every unit by its deadline if and only if, for every
𝑘, cumulative service lies between the work due and the work available:

Proof. See Appendix A.5.
Lemma 2 uses the fact that all spot work of a model has the same relative deadline so that
first-in-first-out order is also earliest-deadline-first order. With heterogeneous deadlines, the same
constraints hold for each deadline class, and the controller would need one queue per class.

of the largest revenue 𝜋ˆΛ/4, which is 0.062% for 𝐾= 40.

(ii) The right-hand side of (20), maximized over 𝑖, is at most the expected overflow and equals it at
the grid points. Between grid points 𝑧𝑖< 𝑧𝑖+1, the gap is at most 𝜎(𝑧𝑖+1 −𝑧𝑖)2𝜙𝑁(0)/4, and for the

Proof. See Appendix A.10.
Therefore, the program slightly understates spot revenue and slightly understates the risk of
interactive overflow. Neither error matters at the resolution of the study. The planned price is
obtained from the demand curve at the planned admissions, i.e., 𝑝𝑚,𝑡= 𝜋𝑚(1 −𝑎𝑚,0/ˆΛ𝑚,0). Since the
optimal admissions usually sit at a breakpoint of ˆΠ𝐾, prices move in ticks of 𝜋𝑚/𝐾, which is 2.5% of
the interactive price for 𝐾= 40.
6.3 The control loop
Algorithm 1 summarizes the closed loop. Two steps convert the plan into actions. First, the planned
replicas are rounded to whole numbers, rounding to the nearest integer where the fleet allows and
down otherwise. Second, the planned price is posted, and buyers decide how much work to submit
at that price. The program learns what buyers actually submitted only in the next period, when
the realized admissions appear in the backlog. Therefore, any gap between planned and realized
demand is absorbed by the queue and corrected by the next plan through feedback.
Relation to the structural results of Section 5. The program (21) contains the four simplified
problems of Section 5 as special cases, and its optimality conditions reproduce their rules. For one
step with 𝐷= 1 and no switching costs, the program reduces to (10), up to the approximations of
Lemma 3, and hence its spot prices are 1
2 (𝜋𝑚+ MC𝑚) with the shadow rent 𝜈𝑘and power price 𝜂𝑘of
that step (Proposition 1). With longer deadlines, the cumulative constraints of Lemma 2 allow work
to move to the cheapest step in its window, and prices follow the effective cost 𝐶𝑡of Theorem 1. The
cuts (20) set the interactive safety margin at the critical fractile of Theorem 2, with the spot tier as
salvage value. In particular, at the optimum, the slope 1 −Φ𝑁(𝑧) of the active cut balances the cost
of a replica against the value of its spot capacity. Moreover, the load and unload costs produce the
inaction band of Theorem 3. The multipliers 𝜇𝑚,𝑘, 𝜈𝑘, and 𝜂𝑘are also useful outputs in their own
right. For example, 𝜌𝑚MC𝑚is a floor for interactive prices, and the effective cost 𝐶𝑡is the provider’s
competitive ask on an exchange (Remark 1).
Size and speed. With 𝑀models and horizon 𝐻, the program has (8 + 𝐾)𝑀𝐻+ 𝐻variables, which
amounts to 2, 320 for 𝑀= 3, 𝐻= 16, and 𝐾= 40, and about 30𝑀𝐻constraints, most of which are

cuts. HiGHS [16] solves it in about 7 milliseconds on a laptop, compared with a control period of 15

7 Numerical study
In this section, we evaluate how much a provider gains from dynamic placement and pricing, where
the gain comes from, and how it depends on forecasts, switching costs, and contract terms. All
numbers come from the scripts listed in Appendix C.
7.1 Setup
Fleet and models. Consider a provider that runs 𝐺= 512 accelerators under a nominal power cap
of 380 kW and serves three models (Table 1). The small model fits on one accelerator, the medium
model on two, and the large mixture-of-experts model on eight. Their batching parameters yield
interactive batch caps between 83 and 133 sequences and exchange rates 𝜌𝑚between 1.24 and 1.51.
Loading weights takes 30, 90, and 300 seconds, which corresponds to 0.03, 0.10, and 0.33 of a
15-minute period. Each load costs $1.00 and each unload $0.50 per accelerator, which accounts for
warm-up energy, drained sequences, and discarded caches. Interactive prices are $0.15, $0.80, and
$3.00 per million tokens. An idle loaded accelerator draws 0.25 kW, a parked one draws 0.06 kW,
and decode at full load adds 0.45 kW.
Demand. Mean interactive load follows the hour-of-day profile of token volume on a public inference
marketplace, computed from 30 days of hourly data, with a peak-to-trough ratio of 2.6 [32]. The
medium model’s profile is shifted by eight hours, as for a second region, and the large model’s daily
swing is half again as large. Weekend load is 0.91 of weekday load. At the mean, interactive traffic
occupies 49% of the fleet on average. Note that real serving traces are bursty around their daily
pattern [42]. Accordingly, load deviates from its mean by a first-order autoregression with coefficient
0.90 and standard deviation 10%, as in (18). Spot demand follows a flatter daily profile with an
independent 10% noise every period, and it is scaled so that, at half the interactive price, it would
occupy 35% of the fleet. Spot work must finish within 𝐷= 8 periods (120 minutes). A lost interactive
token costs 𝛽𝑚= 5 𝜋𝑚in service credits and goodwill, and an expired spot token is refunded and
costs 𝛾𝑚= 0.5 𝜋𝑚.

refers to the best constant placement for two typical weekdays at mean demand.

Electricity and events. Electricity costs $0.065 per kWh on average, with a daily swing of $0.025
that peaks at 20:00 UTC. The simulated week contains two events that the seasonal profile does not
anticipate. On Wednesday, a model launch doubles the large model’s interactive load, ramping up
from 13 : 00 UTC over 1 hour, holding for 5 hours, and decaying over 3 hours. On Friday, the grid
operator calls a demand-response event. From 17 : 00 UTC for 2 hours, the facility must stay below
62% of its nominal cap (236 kW), and electricity costs $0.80 per kWh. The event is announced 2
hours ahead.
Policies. We compare six policies (Table 2). Posted represents current practice, namely, the best
static placement for a typical weekday and a spot tier sold at half the interactive price. It is a strong
version of that practice since the same planning program sets a rate limit on spot admissions so that
the posted tier never accepts more work than it expects to finish by the deadline. Dynamic price
and Dynamic placement each add one of the two levers. Myopic uses both levers with a persistence
forecast, i.e., it expects current interactive load, spot demand, electricity price, and power cap to
continue unchanged. MPC is Algorithm 1 with the forecasts (18) and a horizon of 16 periods (4
hours). Oracle knows the realized future over twice that horizon and bounds what any controller
could achieve with this program.
Simulation. Each policy is run for one week at 15-minute periods on 20 random draws of interactive
load and spot demand, with the same draws for every policy. The plant serves interactive traffic first
at the effective replicas (5), serves spot work first-in-first-out within the capacity (6), and enforces
the power cap by shedding spot work first and interactive work second. Profit is computed by (9)
without the holding cost, which serves as a planning device. Gains are measured against Posted,
paired by draw, and reported with standard errors across draws.
7.2 Results
Profit gain of 7.4% from dynamic control. Table 3 summarizes the week. MPC earns $369.8
thousand, compared with $344.1 thousand for Posted, which is a gain of 7.4% (standard error 0.32),
and it captures 93% of the gain of the Oracle. Of the $25.6 thousand gained per week, $13.3 thousand
comes from interactive penalties avoided, $2.7 thousand from interactive revenue no longer lost,
and $12.2 thousand from additional spot revenue, while switching costs take back $1.6 thousand,
and energy, refunds, and expiry penalties take back $0.9 thousand. In addition, the interactive tier
receives better service. MPC misses the speed promise on 0.01% of interactive tokens, compared
with 0.25% for Posted. Note that the two levers are complements. Dynamic prices alone gain 2.7%,

Prices on ordinary days and placement during events. Figure 9 breaks the gain down by day. On
the five days without events, MPC gains 2.5%, and dynamic prices alone already gain 2.4%. On these
days, the fleet is tight only for a few evening hours. As Proposition 2 predicts, the fixed discount loses
little when capacity is slack, and its losses are concentrated in the tight hours. On the day of the
flash crowd, MPC gains 38.4%, and on the day of the grid event, it gains 7.4%. Prices cannot help
on these days since the interactive tier is the one short of capacity, and only moving accelerators or
power to it can help. Figure 10 shows the week under MPC. Placement follows the daily cycle in
small steps and moves sharply only for the two events. Spot prices stay at or within a tick or two of
half price for most of the week and rise during the events.

peak, compared with a static allocation of 224 (Fig. 11a,b). Since the forecast learns the surge from
the load it observes, the first periods are served from the safety margin. In the first draw, Posted fails
to serve 0.6 billion interactive tokens during the surge, and MPC fails to serve 0.01 billion. Dynamic
prices alone fail to serve 0.6 billion, the same as Posted. The reason is that raising the spot price frees
spot capacity on the large model’s replicas, but the interactive tier needs more replicas rather than
more room on the ones it has. At the same time, MPC raises the spot price of every model, to 0.78
of the interactive price for the large model and to 0.73 and 0.73 for the small and medium ones,
respectively (Fig. 11c). The other models’ prices rise because they gave up accelerators, which is the
spillover of Proposition 1(iv).
The grid event. Two hours before the event, MPC learns that the cap will fall to 236 kW. It raises
spot prices to slow admissions, serves more of the backlog before the event, and, at the start of
the event, unloads replicas to park their accelerators, going from 500 to 322 loaded accelerators
(Fig. 10b). Facility power falls by 111 kW from its level in the two hours before (Fig. 11d). The
interactive tier is served in full throughout, and the spot tier absorbs the curtailment. In particular,
MPC serves 1.2 billion spot tokens in the two hours of the event, compared with 6.9 billion in the
26


--- Page 27 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
two hours before. In contrast, Posted keeps its replicas loaded, cannot fit even its interactive load
under the cap, and loses 1.2 billion interactive tokens in the first draw (0.53 billion on average). The
spot price during the event reaches 0.78 of the interactive price for the large model (Fig. 11f). In
this sense, the spot tier serves as the facility’s flexible load, and its price tells buyers when the facility
is curtailed.
Buyers. Spot buyers are not worse off. Although dynamic prices are above half price in tight hours,
MPC serves more spot work in total. The posted tier rations by a rate limit that is set before demand
is known, and it turns work away whenever demand exceeds the limit. In contrast, a price admits
whatever buyers want at that price and lets the backlog absorb the surprise. Moreover, MPC has
more capacity when it is needed since it moves replicas. It serves 526 billion spot tokens a week,
compared with 495 billion for Posted, and spot buyers’ surplus is 6.5% higher. Profit plus buyer
surplus rises by 7.3%. The cost to buyers is a longer wait. The mean delay of a spot token rises from
11 to 15 minutes, and its 95th percentile rises from 33 to 51 minutes, which is still well within the
120-minute deadline. Only 0.07% of admitted spot work expires. The Oracle waits longest since it
knows best when capacity will be free.
7.3 Sensitivity
In this subsection, we vary one feature at a time on 10 draws, with gains paired by draw against
Posted under the same conditions (Fig. 12).
Lookahead. A controller that plans one period ahead gains 5.5%. Planning one hour ahead gains
6.8%, and planning four hours ahead gains 7.1%, with no further gain from eight hours (Fig. 12a).
A few hours suffice since the deadline is two hours and placement transients last a few hours.
Switching costs and loading time. Without switching costs, MPC gains 7.7% but loads 7, 414
accelerators a week. The base cost cuts loads to 1, 098 for a gain of 7.1%. As the cost rises, placement
freezes (Theorem 3). At 64 times the base cost, the controller loads 6 accelerators a week and gains
2.7%, which is the gain of dynamic prices alone (Fig. 12b). Loading time matters much less than
loading cost. Scaling all load times by 0, 1, 2, and 3 yields gains of 7.2%, 7.1%, 7.1%, and 7.0%,
since the controller loads ahead of need, and the lost fraction of a period matters only when a load is
a surprise.
Deadlines. Longer deadlines raise the profit of both policies (Fig. 12c), as predicted by Theorem 1(iv).
With a deadline of one period, MPC earns $363.6 thousand and Posted $341.0 thousand; with 8
hours, they earn $371.7 thousand and $350.2 thousand, respectively. The gain of MPC over Posted
is 6.6% and 6.1% at the two ends. Deferral and dynamic pricing are partial substitutes since a long
deadline allows even a fixed-price tier to move work out of tight hours. This observation is consistent
with current batch tiers, which pair a fixed discount with a 24-hour window.
Forecast noise. With a standard deviation of interactive-load deviations of 5%, MPC gains 7.3% and
Myopic 6.8%. At 30%, they gain 8.5% and 7.2%, respectively (Fig. 12d). The gain does not shrink
with noise since noise hurts the static policy more. A static placement must cover the unconditional
variation of load, whereas the controller re-plans every period and sizes its margin to the error of a
forecast a few periods ahead, which is much smaller when deviations persist. Both sell their margins
as spot capacity, as in Theorem 2.

8 Discussion
In this section, we discuss the implications of our results, their implementation, and their limitations.
Implications for providers. Four operating rules follow from Section 5, and each of them continues
to hold in the closed loop of Section 7.
1. Price spot work midway between the interactive price and its effective cost. The effective cost 𝐶𝑡is
the cheapest cost of serving the work anywhere in its deadline window, including the shadow rent
of the fleet and of power in that period (Theorem 1). When the fleet is slack, the resulting spot
price is close to the prevailing half price (Proposition 1(v)). When the fleet is tight, the price is
higher, and it is higher for every model at once since the models share the fleet.
2. Price interactive service above 𝜌𝑚MC𝑚. An interactive token displaces 𝜌𝑚spot tokens (Lemma 1),
and hence the shadow cost of interactive capacity is the spot cost scaled by the latency exchange
rate (Proposition 1(ii)). A provider that prices its fast tiers off its standard tier by a fixed multiple
ignores the scarcity of the fleet.
28


--- Page 29 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
3. Hold more safety capacity when a spot tier can use it. Spot work serves as the salvage market for the
interactive tier’s safety margin, and hence the optimal probability of missing the speed promise
falls as the spot tier becomes more valuable (Theorem 2). In other words, the spot tier and the
interactive tier’s reliability are complements rather than rivals.
4. Price the transients and place the trends. Move weights only when the cumulative value of a replica
over the expected duration of a shift exceeds the round-trip cost of loading and unloading it
(Theorem 3). Absorb shorter shifts with the spot price and the backlog.
Implementation. The controller requires forecasts of means and standard deviations, the current
backlog with its deadlines, and the announced electricity prices and power caps. Its program is a
linear program of a few thousand variables that solves in milliseconds, and hence it can run every
few minutes alongside an existing batch scheduler. Note that the scheduler needs no change. It
serves interactive traffic first and fills the remaining slots with spot work in first-in-first-out order,
which is what continuous-batching servers already do with priorities. Moreover, the spot price can be
published as a schedule over the next few hours, which informs buyers of when capacity is likely to
be cheap and when the facility expects to curtail.
Market power and the half-price rule. Our provider is a monopolist of its own spare capacity
facing linear demand, and the factor 1
2 in the pricing rules comes from that demand curve. With
other valuation distributions, the markup over 𝐶𝑡changes, but the cost side of every result does not.
In particular, the shadow prices of the fleet and power, the effective cost under deferral, the critical
fractile, and the inaction band are properties of the provider’s operations rather than of its demand.
If the provider sold its spare capacity on a competitive exchange, it would ask 𝐶𝑡itself (Remark 1),
and the difference between the monopoly price and 𝐶𝑡measures the provider’s market power over its
spot tier.
The spot tier as flexible load. Grid operators increasingly ask large new loads to curtail during the
few hours a year when the grid is stressed [25]. The grid event of Section 7 shows that a spot tier
makes such curtailment cheap for an inference provider. The interactive tier keeps its promise, and
the curtailment falls on work whose buyers accepted a deadline and are compensated for it through a
lower price. The shadow price 𝜂of power in the planning program represents the provider’s value of
a kilowatt at each hour. A provider could use it to bid its flexibility into a demand-response program,
which would turn the spot tier’s flexibility into revenue from the grid as well as from buyers.
Limitations. The model is a fluid model. It summarizes batching by full-load throughputs and does
not track the latency of individual requests, the split between prefill and decode, or the memory
of key–value caches beyond the batch cap. It treats interactive demand as exogenous in the short
run and spot buyers as price-takers who do not time their submissions against the price schedule.
Moreover, forecast errors are normal, and there is one facility with one kind of accelerator. The
planning program is solved by receding horizon without closed-loop guarantees. In addition, the
numerical study is stylized. Its daily profile is measured, but its fleet, models, prices, and events are
illustrative, and hence its percentages indicate magnitudes rather than predict a provider’s results.
Each of these limitations points to a direction for further work. Possible directions include several
facilities with transfer between them, as in Zhang et al. [47]; prefill and decode as two resources;
demand curves learned online; buyers who choose deadlines from a menu of prices; and robust or
stochastic versions of the program.
29


--- Page 30 ---
quanyan zhu
Spot Markets for AI Inference
9 Conclusion
Inference providers operate fleets sized for the interactive peak and sell the remaining capacity
through fixed discounts. In this paper, we have developed a framework for allocating and pricing
this capacity dynamically. Four features distinguish inference from conventional cloud capacity:
capacity depends on the latency tier, placement is slow and costly while the split between tiers is free,
demand can wait until a deadline, and power can bind. We have shown that, when these features
are taken into account, the provider’s problem has a clear structure. Spot prices lie midway between
the interactive price and the effective cost of capacity in the deadline window. Interactive capacity
carries a shadow cost scaled by the latency exchange rate. A spot tier raises the optimal reliability
of the interactive tier. Placement should follow persistent shifts in demand and leave transients to
prices. Building on these elements, we have designed a model predictive controller that solves a
small linear program each period. In a simulated week, the controller raises profit by 7.4% over a
fixed half-price policy, captures 93% of the gain available with perfect forecasts, keeps the interactive
promise through a flash crowd and a grid curtailment, and leaves spot buyers better off.
More broadly, the analysis suggests that the price of spare inference capacity should be understood
as an operational signal rather than a fixed discount. This price summarizes, at each moment, the
scarcity of accelerators, the cost and availability of power, and the flexibility that buyers offer through
their deadlines. As inference becomes a basic input to economic activity and a significant load on the
power grid, mechanisms that make this signal explicit will matter for the efficiency of AI services
and for their integration with the energy system. As future work, we would extend the framework
to facilities linked by transfers of work, to prefill and decode as separate resources, and to demand
curves learned online. Other directions include buyers who choose deadlines strategically from a
menu of prices and competition among providers whose spot tiers serve overlapping buyers.
Appendix A Proofs
In this appendix, we prove the results of Sections 4 to 6. Section A.1 collects the facts that the proofs
use. The proofs then follow in the order in which the results appear, except that Lemma 2 is proved
before Theorem 1, which uses it, and Remark 1 is proved after Theorem 3.
A.1 Preliminaries
Supergradients and optimality conditions. For a concave function 𝑉on ℝ, 𝜕𝑉(𝑛) = {𝑤: 𝑉(𝑚) ≤
𝑉(𝑛) + 𝑤(𝑚−𝑛) ∀𝑚} denotes its superdifferential, which is the interval between the right and left
derivatives of 𝑉at 𝑛. Note that all optimization problems below maximize a concave objective
subject to linear constraints. For such problems, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, with
supergradients in place of gradients where the objective is not differentiable, are necessary at an
optimum without any further constraint qualification, and they are sufficient for optimality [36,
Sections 28–29]. We use this fact without further mention.
Decode throughput. With 𝜏𝑚(𝑏) = 𝜏0,𝑚+ 𝜏1,𝑚𝑏and 𝜃𝑚(𝑏) = 𝑏/𝜏𝑚(𝑏),

𝜏0,𝑚

A.5 Proof of Lemma 2 (deadlines as cumulative constraints)
We order the units of work by deadline, breaking ties by admission time. Since all work has the same
relative deadline 𝐷, this order is the order of admission, and hence first-in-first-out service removes
units in this order. Let 𝑋𝑘= Í
𝑗≤𝑘(𝑥𝑗+ 𝑧𝑗) denote the cumulative work removed by the end of step 𝑘.
Under first-in-first-out, the units removed by step 𝑘are exactly the first 𝑋𝑘units in the order. The
work due by step 𝑘consists of the old backlog due by then, 𝑑𝑘, plus the work admitted at steps 𝑗with
𝑗+ 𝐷−1 ≤𝑘. Every unit due by 𝑘is removed by 𝑘if and only if 𝑋𝑘is at least this amount, which is the
left inequality. The right inequality states that no more work is removed than has arrived. Conversely,
any nondecreasing 𝑋that satisfies both inequalities for all 𝑘is realized by first-in-first-out service of
𝑋𝑘−𝑋𝑘−1 units at step 𝑘.
□

(ii) If Δ𝜃S𝑣< 𝑘, then Φ′(𝑛) →Δ𝑣𝜃S −𝑘< 0 as 𝑛→∞, while Φ′(0) = Δ(𝜋+ 𝛽)𝜃I −𝑘> 0 when
𝐹(0) = 0, by the assumption on 𝑘. For a load distribution with support on the whole line, such as
the normal in (iv), we let 𝑛range over ℝ, and Φ′(𝑛) →Δ(𝜋+ 𝛽)𝜃I −𝑘> 0 as 𝑛→−∞. Since 𝐹is
continuous, Φ′(𝑛∗) = 0 for some 𝑛∗, which is optimal by concavity. Solving for ¯𝐹(𝜃I𝑛∗) and dividing
the numerator and the denominator by 𝜃I yields (16).
(iii) We write 𝜛(𝑣) = (𝐴−𝜌𝑣)/(𝐵−𝜌𝑣) with 𝐴= 𝑘/(Δ𝜃I) and 𝐵= 𝜋+ 𝛽. The assumption on 𝑘is
equivalent to 𝐴< 𝐵, and 𝜛′(𝑣) = 𝜌(𝐴−𝐵)/(𝐵−𝜌𝑣)2 < 0. At 𝑣= 0, 𝜛= 𝐴/𝐵.
(iv) If 𝑅∼𝑁(ˆ𝑟, 𝜎2), then ¯𝐹(𝜃I𝑛∗) = 𝜛gives 𝜃I𝑛∗= ˆ𝑟+ 𝑧∗𝜎. The expected spot capacity is
Δ𝜃S 𝔼(𝑛∗−𝑅/𝜃I)+ = Δ𝜌𝔼(𝜃I𝑛∗−𝑅)+ = Δ𝜌𝜎𝔼(𝑧∗−𝑍)+ with 𝑍standard normal, and 𝔼(𝑧−𝑍)+ =
𝑧Φ𝑁(𝑧) + 𝜙𝑁(𝑧). Since 𝑧∗does not depend on 𝜎, the capacity is proportional to 𝜎.
□

We write (17) with loads 𝑢𝑡≥0 and unloads 𝑣𝑡≥0, 𝑛𝑡−𝑛𝑡−1 = 𝑢𝑡−𝑣𝑡, and objective Í

contains a point 𝑤𝑡∈[0, 𝛿]. With these choices, 𝜉𝑡∈[0, 𝑑𝛿] ⊆[−𝜅−, 𝜅+] when 𝑑𝛿≤𝜅+. If plans must
return to ¯𝑛, we add the terminal transition from 𝑛𝑇−1 to 𝑛𝑇= ¯𝑛with its own load and unload costs. Its
multiplier 𝜉𝑇is then free in [−𝜅−, 𝜅+] instead of zero. Choosing 𝜉𝑇= −𝜅−gives 𝜉𝑡∈[−𝜅−, −𝜅−+ 𝑑𝛿],
which lies in [−𝜅−, 𝜅+] when 𝑑𝛿≤𝜅+ + 𝜅−.

A.10 Proof of Lemma 3 (approximation error)
(i) The marginal revenues 𝜋(1−(2𝑗−1)/𝐾) decrease in 𝑗, and hence an optimal split fills the segments

Appendix C Reproducibility
The code is available in spot/code/. The script spotsim.py contains the model, the planning program
(21), the forecasts, and the plant. The script concept.py computes the examples of Sections 4 to 6,
writes Table 1 and the macros quoted in those sections, and draws Figs. 3 and 5 to 8. The script
run.py runs every simulation of Section 7, 510 weeks in all, in about fifteen minutes on a ten-core
laptop. The script report.py converts its output into Table 3 and Figs. 9 to 12, and it writes every
number quoted in Section 7. Linear programs are solved by HiGHS [16] through SciPy. The hour-
of-day profile of interactive load is read from data/derived_hod_profile.json, which holds the
mean share of daily token volume in each hour, computed from 30 days of hourly candles of a public
inference marketplace [32]. The tier price ratios quoted in Section 2 are medians over the tiered
endpoints in a snapshot of a model router’s public listings taken on 31 October 2026 [28]. No other
external data are used.
